*   **Accumulated Gradient $\mathbf{g}_i$:** A 2D vector $(g_{i,x}, g_{i,y})$ storing the sum of gradients with respect to the projected screen-space mean $\mu_i$ across all views.

*Note:* The global mean contribution $\bar{w}_i$ used in the final score is typically the sum of per-view means or the mean over all pixels across all views, depending on the specific implementation variant.
*   **Cloning Over-densification:** The clone operation (creating a new Gaussian at the same position) can cause catastrophic over-densification and inflated counts without quality improvement.
*   **Occlusion Bias:** Normalizing by raw view count $M$ (as in standard 3DGS) includes occluded views where the gradient is zero, dragging down the average and stalling densification.
*   **Footprint Bias:** Using the per-view total weight $\sum_p w_{i,p}$ as the normalizer reintroduces pixel-count dependence, as larger footprints accumulate more weight.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot P \cdot V)$, where $N$ is the number of Gaussians, $P$ is the average number of pixels per Gaussian footprint, and $V$ is the number of views.
The normalization step is $O(V)$ per Gaussian.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N \cdot V)$ to store accumulated gradients and contribution sums if not computed on the fly.
The method was developed to address the limitations of view-count normalization in the presence of occlusions, which is common in complex scenes.
It builds on the observation that the gradient signal is intrinsically contribution-weighted, making the mean contribution a natural normalizer.
